statement: A coach says: 'Everyone who made the team came to every practice.' If the coach is right, which of the following must be true?

choices.text: Ana came to every practice, so she made the team.
choices.misconception: I reversed the statement, as if coming to every practice guaranteed a place on the team.

choices.text: Ben missed a practice, so he did not make the team.
Cleo did not make the team, so she missed a practice.
choices.misconception: I assumed not making the team means a missed practice, but Cleo may have come every time and still not been picked.

choices.text: Everyone who came to every practice made the team.
choices.misconception: I turned 'everyone who made the team came' into 'everyone who came made the team'.

choices.text: At least one person made the team.
choices.misconception: I assumed the statement says someone made the team, but it would still be true if nobody did.

hints: Which kind of person would make the coach wrong?
A statement of the form 'everyone who is P is Q' is broken only by someone who is P but not Q. For each choice, ask whether it could fail while the coach is still right.
If Ben missed a practice and made the team anyway, the coach would be wrong.

solutions.reliable: The coach's claim says there is nobody who made the team but missed a practice. Ben missed a practice, so if he had made the team the claim would be false; hence he did not make the team, and B must be true. A and D reverse the claim. C fails because Cleo could have come to every practice and still not been picked. E fails because the claim is also true if nobody made the team. The transferable idea: 'every P is Q' also means 'not Q means not P', but it does not mean 'Q means P'.

whyOnTest: Reading 'everyone who ...' precisely: the contrapositive must hold, while the reversed statement and its opposite are the common traps.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
